section_summary: This section begins with the end of an assessment of Japan’s implementation of FEC-230, the proposed policy on excessive concentrations of economic power. The remaining documents trace State and Army Department disagreements over revising or withdrawing the proposal, the possible effects on Japan’s recovery, and how the United States should respond as the Far Eastern Commission prepares its own policy statement. Draft policies, internal comments, a telegram, and a newspaper clipping accompany the memoranda.

subfiles.title: Assessment of Japanese implementation of FEC-230
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese laws and occupation measures against articles of the proposed deconcentration policy.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion assesses divestiture, finance, government support for monopolies, corporate and tax law, public education, and safeguards for foreign interests. It distinguishes measures already enacted from proposals still incomplete or unsupported by evidence. A list of Japanese laws and ordinances consulted closes the report.

subfiles.title: Review of FEC-230
subfiles.about: Records a January 10 State–Army meeting on revising FEC-230 and possibly sending a mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gray questioned whether a revised policy was needed after recent Japanese laws and proposed a mission. State officials argued that delay would damage the deconcentration program and pressed for prompt review of the laws and a decision on a substitute paper.

subfiles.title: Revised FEC-230
subfiles.about: Urges an approach to Gray to secure Army support for a revised FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: Whitman argues that a mission need not delay a general policy statement and that State has already promised a revision. He outlines how the agreed draft could move through SANACC and the Far Eastern Commission while preserving time for further review.

subfiles.title: FEC-230
subfiles.about: Explains why the United States cannot unilaterally withdraw FEC-230 from the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Withdrawal requires a Commission decision, though the United States may propose amendments or change its position.

subfiles.title: Proposed revisions of ‘Policy on Excessive Concentrations of Economic Power in Japan’
subfiles.about: Recommends draft changes responding to Gray’s comments on the proposed policy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum proposes clearer standards and exceptions for efficiency and utilities, plus provisions on small business and public information. It explains why broader divestiture rules should remain and answers Gray’s objections about compensation, technical assistance, and patents.

subfiles.title: Comments on proposed policy on excessive concentrations of economic power
subfiles.about: Comments on the January 10 draft policy and questions its definitions and proposed remedies.
subfiles.summary: The comments ask for clearer thresholds and geographic scope, safeguards for public utilities and viable firms, and less forceful language. They also question provisions on divestiture, patents, small business, and public education.

subfiles.title: Appendix C: Policy on excessive concentrations of economic power in Japan
subfiles.about: Sets out a proposed replacement policy for dissolving and preventing excessive economic concentrations.
subfiles.summary: The draft defines excessive concentration and calls for separating firms while protecting operating efficiency, compensating affected individuals, and dispersing ownership and credit. It addresses financial alliances, monopoly support, corporate and patent law, small business, public support, government personnel, and foreign interests.

subfiles.title: Reasons for continuing with FEC-230
subfiles.about: Argues that the United States should continue Far Eastern Commission consideration of FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: Claxton warns that abandonment would weaken SCAP’s apparent support, increase uncertainty in Japan, and embarrass State before Congress and the Commission. The memorandum says withdrawal needs Commission consent; page 161 repeats part of the withdrawal argument.

subfiles.title: FEC 230; The Strike Report
subfiles.about: Calls for Army discussion of replacing FEC-230 and preparation for the Strike Report.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman favors a substitute policy and urges attention to Japanese industry and reparations before the Strike Report arrives.

subfiles.title: Zaibatsu Program (FEC 230) and Proposed Army Sponsored Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper report of MacArthur’s support for deconcentration.
subfiles.summary: Wisner highlights MacArthur’s public backing for the policy amid congressional criticism and mission discussions.

subfiles.title: MacArthur Backs Policy of Trust-Busting
subfiles.from: Jack Werkley, New York Herald Tribune
subfiles.about: Reports MacArthur’s letter defending the breakup of Japanese economic concentrations.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur tells Senator McMahon that deconcentration is essential to a competitive Japanese economy and democratic stability.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Mitsubishi property sales
subfiles.about: Reports a pause in sales of Mitsubishi properties pending Tidewater Oil representatives’ arrival.
subfiles.summary: Sales are held up; two Tidewater Oil representatives have been cleared to enter Japan.

subfiles.title: Secretary Royall’s Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Reviews the purpose, membership, and policy implications of Royall’s planned mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wisner reports possible mission members and seeks clarity about whether they will make a formal policy report or serve as Royall’s personal advisers. He recommends discussing the mission’s scope and State Department participation with Royall.

subfiles.title: Comment on ‘Handling of FEC-230’
subfiles.about: Comments on Whitman’s proposed handling of FEC-230 and its draft policy language.
subfiles.summary: Fearey favors working on an acceptable Commission paper over a veto or further delay. He offers specific wording changes on efficiency, timing, legal enforcement, and other provisions, and raises the need for Army clearance.

subfiles.title: My Memorandum of June 2 Entitled ‘Handling of FEC-230 at the FEC’
subfiles.about: Proposes parallel U.S. and Far Eastern Commission consideration of a draft deconcentration policy.
subfiles.summary: Whitman suggests sounding out Army, submitting the draft to SANACC and an FEC subcommittee, and incorporating later SCAP comments before a Commission vote. He expects Commission deliberations to provide time for U.S. clearance.

subfiles.title: Handling of FEC-230 at the FEC
subfiles.about: Compares three U.S. responses to the Commission’s decision to draft a shorter FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: Whitman rejects an announced veto and further delaying tactics as politically damaging and unlikely to stop drafting. He recommends informal U.S. participation in the subcommittee, using an attached shorter statement as the basis for discussion.

subfiles.title: Comment on ‘Handling of FEC 230’
subfiles.about: Objects to introducing an unapproved U.S. draft in the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton calls for Army concurrence and a brief paper grounded in existing Japanese law and approved occupation policy.

subfiles.title: Proposed Handling of FEC-230
subfiles.about: Reviews comments on Whitman’s proposal and recommends a route for Army consultation.
subfiles.summary: Allison reports that British, Australian, and New Zealand representatives expect a Commission policy decision but favor a short statement of principles. He would send Whitman’s draft to Army for comment while withholding any U.S. presentation to the Commission until government approval.

subfiles.title: Attached package on deconcentration policy
subfiles.about: Forwards advance copies of memoranda and a proposed deconcentration statement.
subfiles.summary: Owen lists the enclosed policy package and promises a revised account of actions taken.

subfiles.title: FEC Policy Paper on Deconcentration
subfiles.about: Reassesses U.S. options after Army objections to a new deconcentration paper.
subfiles.summary: Whitman recounts proposals to give the Commission an account of Japanese actions and, if necessary, an agreed short policy statement. Draper opposed a new paper and favored a veto. Whitman recommends seeking the Secretary’s approval before pressing the issue with Army leaders.

subfiles.title: Proposed U.S. action on a Far Eastern Commission deconcentration statement
subfiles.about: Seeks approval to press Army for a U.S. approach to the Commission’s deconcentration paper.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman proposes first explaining SCAP’s actions to the Commission and arguing that a new policy is unnecessary. If the Commission proceeds, its statement should match a U.S. approved draft. He seeks authority to raise the proposal with Royall if Draper rejects it.

subfiles.title: Policy with Respect to Excessive Concentrations of Economic Power in Japan
subfiles.about: Begins a proposed policy defining excessive concentration and the principles for ending it.
subfiles.summary: The opening page calls for wider industrial ownership, effective separation of concentrated firms, protection of efficiency, public support, and a June 1949 target for announcing measures. The draft continues beyond this section.
